claims.text: The starting coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure with a natural phase fraction and distribution.
Increasing the density of FCC/BCC phase boundaries improves creep resistance.
Increasing the strength of FCC/BCC phase boundaries improves creep resistance.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries impede dislocation motion during continuous loading.
Processing conditions can be modified to increase FCC/BCC boundary density or connectivity without changing the overall chemical composition.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries act as dislocation-pinning sites.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries restrict dislocation glide.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries restrict dislocation climb.
Restricting dislocation glide and climb slows progressive creep deformation.
A coating with increased FCC/BCC interfacial density will have a lower creep rate than the original coating under the same sustained stress and temperature.
Operational conditions for the coating can include sustained loading at temperatures up to approximately 600 degrees Celsius.
The proposed effect is expected where creep dominates at sustained high temperatures and moderate-to-high stresses.
The proposed effect is expected for coatings with similar bulk chemical compositions.
The quantitative creep-rate effect depends on interactions among dislocation density, phase fraction, and detailed microstructural arrangement.
